text: Rein leather is the same as harness leather in every respect, except that instead of being colored black it is bleached and afterwards stained brown or some other color.
Cuir-color is a very light, almost imperceptible brown produced by bleaching rein leather quite light and then coloring it with a yellowish-brown stain.
The cuir-color shade is nearer to the natural color of fine oak-tanned leather than anything else, and the stain serves more to produce a uniform shade than to establish a new color.
When cuir-color is used, very little stain is needed on the edges of straps to bring them up to the same shade as the grain.
The beauty of a russet rein depends as much on its uniformity of color as on its make, so the harness maker should get from the leather manufacturer the same stain that was used to color the grain.
Brown and yellow stains can be made very easily, but the stains for soft, fine shades are kept secret by leather manufacturers until fashion adopts a new favorite color.
Short-tanned rein leather takes a less uniform shade when stained, because the untanned center shows darker than the portion well filled with bark.
Poor rein leather works harder, does not keep its shape as well, and if the grain is hard it is liable to crack while being made up or when bent in use.
A pair of russet reins contains about one pound of leather.
Because a pair of russet reins holds only about one pound of leather, the saving from using the lowest priced stock is trifling and does not justify the danger of unsafe reins.
Hand-part leather should be of the very best quality, soft and pliant, and it can be judged by the same tests as other leather.

Cutting the folds for hand parts from the same side as the rounds is a mistake, because rein leather is usually too heavy for folds and must be split, which removes some of the strongest part of the leather and takes the workman's time.
Hand-part leather made expressly for the purpose is lighter, much stronger in proportion to its thickness, and ready to make up once cut to width.

For flat hand parts the leather should be as heavy as that used for the rounds; it can be cut from the same sides, but it is generally too hard and must be softened, for example by pulling it around a post or rolling and working it.
Grained leather is quite popular for flat hand parts and looks well.
To grain hand-part leather in the workshop, cut a piece wide enough for two pairs of hand parts, because a piece wide enough for one pair is too narrow to work well.

To board hand-part leather, lay the strip grain side up on a table and crease the grain with a currier's board, starting at the front corner of one end and giving a half roll diagonally across the strip to the other end. Then start at the front corner of the other end and board back at the same angle, so the creases cross each other.
In boarded hand-part leather the fineness of the graining depends on the amount of labor applied.
Graining hand-part leather by boarding also breaks down and softens the leather, making it as pliant as can be desired.
Buff leather is leather of the same stock as other hand-part leather that is not stained; the currier buffs the grain to remove the gloss and give it a white, furried appearance.
Buff leather is one of the best kinds for hand parts because it is soft and pliant, looks well, and will not soil the most delicate fabrics.
Loop leather is a light-colored leather that is not curried with oil, or is curried with only a very small quantity of grease.
Loop leather must be solid and yet have a mellow grain that readily takes a crease and retains it.

A test of loop leather: if one crease mark placed close to another obliterates it or lessens its depth, a good piece of work cannot be made. With a mellow grain each impression of the creaser becomes permanently set and the adjoining one stays equally well defined.
The tests for selecting a side of loop leather are good tannage, a mellow grain and a solid body.
In loop leather a lack of uniform thickness is an advantage: shoulders and other thin parts serve for check and other light loops, and the thick butts for trace and similar heavy loops.
Weight stock is sold by the pound, with the weight ascertained at the time of sale.
Trimmed stock is marked with its weight while in the rough, and after trimming and currying there is no means of checking whether the brand is correct.
It is claimed that a side of leather weighing eighteen pounds in the rough loses about four pounds in currying and trimming.
The estimate that a side loses about four pounds in currying cannot be relied on, because a currier can stuff badly fleshed leather with cheap oil until the finished weight equals the rough weight.
Backs and trimmed sides are sold by the rough weight, with an additional charge of $1 and $1.50 each for dressing.
A leading New York manufacturer adopted the plan of selling backs by their actual weight at the time of sale, at 82 cents per pound.
The buyer of a back may take or leave the bellies; if left, their value by weight is deducted from the bill. The bellies weigh, as a rule, four pounds.

A side weighing eighteen pounds in the rough, if properly fleshed and curried, loses four pounds in that process and three or four pounds more by cropping, leaving about eleven pounds of prime leather in the back.

In buying a back by rough weight, 48 cents a pound is charged for eighteen pounds and $1.50 is added for dressing; after deducting for the bellies the total cost is $8.70 for about eleven pounds of prime leather, or about 80 cents a pound, nearly double the apparent quotation.
With trimmed stock the buyer pays for the bellies as well as the backs, and the price per pound is about 2 cents less than for backs of the same quality.
An eighteen-pound side of trimmed stock costs $8.28 and actually weighs about fourteen pounds, so the leather costs about 59 cents a pound, about 21 cents a pound less than leather bought as backs.
Any false branding of the rough weight causes a marked advance in the real price of trimmed stock, so it should be bought from honest, reliable men and not from speculators offering low prices.
